_meta.description: Shelved project archive. Aperion drove a Benro Polaris mount, a Canon EOS body, and an offline plate solver from one app — until a firmware patch turned out to be the better answer. Never shipped; kept online as a write-up.
_title: Aperion - Shelved: Deep-Sky Astrophotography for Apple
a-traditional-two-star.3f22a0: A traditional two-star alignment requires you to manually slew to known stars and confirm them. Aperion's auto-align is a closed loop: it captures a frame, plate-solves it offline to figure out exactly where the mount is pointing, syncs the mount to that coordinate, then slews the residual error toward your target. It repeats until the target is centered. You tap once and walk away.
aperion-relied-on-an.e13ba1: Aperion relied on an unofficial control path that neither Benro nor App Review had reason to bless. Patching the mount's own firmware turned out to be the better fix.
aperion-shot-a-frame.4a3569: Aperion shot a frame, plate-solved it on the device and nudged the mount until the target sat in the middle. No internet, and no two-star alignment.

canon-eos-bodies-that.944adf: Canon EOS bodies that support CCAPI (tested on the R5 Mark II with firmware 1.2) are the first-class path and connect over the mount's Wi-Fi hotspot. Other bodies — Nikon, Sony, Fuji, Olympus — connect via libgphoto2 over USB tether. The iPhone's own camera is also a supported capture source.

no-it-was-planned.0243c2: No. It was planned as a one-time $9.99 universal purchase, but it never reached the App Store and it has been shelved — it isn't maintained and there's no build to install. If you want Polaris automation today, use the Benro Polaris Firmware Patcher instead. It's open source, it's free, and it runs on the mount itself.
one-app-drove-a.45249e: One app drove a tracking mount, a camera and an offline plate solver. It never shipped, and the idea lives on in open-source firmware.

the-polaris-exposes-a.e65e70: The Polaris exposes a Wi-Fi hotspot that your iPhone has to join in order to talk to the camera. That would normally cut your phone off from cellular and from the watch, but Aperion uses WatchConnectivity over Bluetooth so the watch keeps full control of the mount, the camera, and the plate-solve trigger regardless of what network the phone is on.

yes-the-star-catalog.db4ae9: Yes. The star catalog and the pattern matcher are bundled inside the app and run on-device. There are no astrometry.net round-trips, no API keys, and no rate limits. Solves work on the mount's air-gapped Wi-Fi network at a remote dark site with no cellular signal.
